en: When ice absorbs heat from its surroundings, its water molecules gain energy and vibrate faster until the solid structure breaks into liquid water.
Sunlight heats a rain puddle, giving surface water molecules enough energy to break free from the liquid and escape into the air as water vapor.
Warm, moist air touching a cold glass of juice loses heat, causing invisible water vapor to slow down and clump together into visible liquid droplets.
When you stir sugar into hot tea, the water molecules pull individual sugar molecules away from the crystal, spreading them evenly to form a solution.
When iron nails are exposed to oxygen and liquid water, a chemical reaction occurs that transforms the shiny metal into a flaky, reddish-brown substance called rust.
Mixing baking soda and vinegar causes an acid-base chemical reaction that rapidly produces carbon dioxide gas, creating the bubbles you see fizzing and overflowing.
When hot sunlight heats a metal bridge, the metal atoms vibrate faster and push further apart, causing the entire structure to expand slightly.
Because pumice rock contains many trapped air bubbles, its overall density is lower than water, causing it to float while solid iron sinks.
Placing liquid water in a freezer removes heat energy, causing the moving water molecules to slow down and lock into a rigid, crystalline solid structure.
Pouring muddy water through filter paper separates the mixture because the tiny pores allow liquid to pass through while trapping larger solid dirt particles.
Adding egg yolk to oil and vinegar allows the mixture to blend smoothly, because the yolk acts as an emulsifier that binds the unmixable liquids together.
Placing a celery stalk in colored water draws the liquid upward through tiny plant tubes, because water molecules stick to the tube walls and to each other.
